title: The nature of the flesh in Romans 7
english: The divine apostle, a tireless model for those following him, for whose sake he cried out: 'become imitators of me, even as I of Christ' (Rom 7:15-17). Truly, what he said is not his own according to the literal word; but I know that the good does not dwell in my flesh, nor is the wretched man I am able to rescue myself from this body of death (Rom 7:18-24).

But he says these things and such things while acting in a parenthetical persona for the purpose of rebuking those who love sin. Just as the divine Scripture knows how to call men by various names—carnal, spiritual, pneumatic, and myriads of others—based on their fleshly deeds, so also it knows how to call the devil not only Satan, adversary, accuser, serpent, and lion, but also Beelzebub, but also flesh, law, sin, and death; for through disobedience we served these, and not Christ.

For this reason he says: 'when we were in the flesh' (Rom 7:7), indicating that they are no longer in the flesh, even though they are in the flesh, so that he is not slandering the flesh in which we are surrounded, but the flesh so named in common, from which we have been set free because we died in Christ through being buried with him through baptism.

Truly we have been freed from this flesh; for he says: 'but now we have been released from the law of sin, having died in that in which we were held, so that we might serve in the newness of the spirit and not in the oldness of the letter' (Rom 7:6).

If he began again by assuming a persona, starting from the point of 'What then shall we say? Is the law sin? By no means!' (Rom 7:7) until 'how shall I be rescued from this body of death?' setting an unshakeable foundation in a prologue for his own defense, saying thus: 'What then? Is the law sin? By no means, but the law is holy, and the commandment is holy, and just, and good.' Here he speaks of law, not the one opposing the law of our mind, but the exhortatory one, the one punishing sinners, for which reason he also judged him to be holy, and just, and good.

If he then began again to resolve following what he said above, having prepared a gracious introduction thus: 'I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord.' Then, for the condemnation of such things being formed and reviled which we surround with flesh, he says interrogatively: 'Am I then I myself serving God by law with my mind, but serving sin by law with my flesh?' (Rom 7:22) 'Am I also Paul, divided, in one way serving the law of God, in another way serving the law of sin?' 'Do I have Christ and Beelzebub together in myself at the same time?' 'Am I he who says: But I no longer live, but Christ lives in me (Gal 2:20), having lied that I have the living sin in myself?'

Addressing others: 'Do you not know that your bodies are a temple of the Holy Spirit in you (1 Cor 6:19), and glorify God in your members?' 'Am I myself having nothing good in the body?' But he is not such a person, he is not; by no means; for he was before a child of wrath and a vessel of wrath, having changed his manner and not his nature, and became a vessel of election, precious.

Since therefore the personified words suit neither the divinely-inspired Paul, nor even certainly everyone united to Christ through baptism, because they were freed from the so-called flesh; for such as these shall no longer be condemned because of the disobedience of Adam (Rom 5:12), sin no longer reigns over them, nor death through sin; for they joined the life of Christ through obedience to the disobedience.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
baehrens: PG Fragmenta in Epistolam ad Romanos u01-open

title: The Law, Sin, and the Deceiver
english: Having abolished the death that happened to us through his own voluntary death, for he willingly became subject to the law of disobedience, so that he might ransom us who are under the law of condemnation (Rom 6:14). For this reason he said, all are redeemed (Rom 6:23); thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord; for the impossibility of the law, in which he was weak through the flesh, God, having sent his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, condemned sin in the flesh (Rom 8:3).

Since this is so well perceived, the divine apostle brings it forth, saying: there is therefore no condemnation to those in Christ Jesus (Rom 8:1); for the law of the spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set me free from the law of sin and death, and from the things of these (Rom 8:2). I will indeed test through brief words and by speaking the words spoken by way of personification, beginning from the [...] and sin, having taken its occasion through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me (Rom 7:7).

The name of sin does not indicate a substance existing, but a manner and a way of having sinned by someone against what is according to reason and right in a matter; for sin is a most general name, being accused according to many and diverse things. And every sin happens neither by word nor by a commanding law; for if it happened according to law and word rightly, it would no longer be defined as sin and having the reason of its generation.

Since, however, the divine apostle remembers not simply sins, but a sin having a most general disposition, having a law, being able to act craftily, providing occasions for the construction of evil, he names no other sin more generally than the deceiver himself, the beginning and father of sins. For the sake of whom the apostle declared that sin reigns: let not sin reign in your mortal body (Rom 6:14). Just as we call men by the art from which they practice, so also he calls the deceiver himself sin, having become first the inventor of sin. Since, therefore, through the commandment given to Adam he deceived man, and through it Adam, providing occasions through the commandment. And this is it: why is it, he says, that God said: from every tree of that in the paradise you shall not eat for food? (Gen 2:16-17). And on whatever day you eat of it, your eyes shall be opened, and you shall be like gods, knowing good and evil (Gen 3:5). But he acts craftily toward them with a greater promise to suppress the deception, promising the more, so that he might turn the keepers of the commandment from the steps of virtue by a fall similar to their own; for having diverted man to want to become equal to God, he provided the occasion for the fellowship of deception from the commandment provided. For this reason Paul said: and sin, having taken its occasion through the commandment, deceived me (Rom 7:7). In order that some might not blame the commandment or the God who gave it, he also used a similar expression, saying: we know that the law is holy and the commandment is holy and just and (Rom 7:13).
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Essence of Sin and the Law
english: It is good. Since, therefore, sin itself—that is, the devil—is sin by nature and by essence, he proffers this: that through the commandment, sin becomes a sin in excess. For that which is by essence cannot receive more or less; for it is what it is, always being what it is essentially. For whatever is added or increased, whether a little or in excess, is of a different essence from the things to which it is added; for 'how much' is not essence, but is about essence, not being essence. Thus, the so-called sin by the apostle, which is received to sin in excess, is so that sin becomes a sin in excess. Thus, even the being of sin, in which it is sin, took its beginning, not being in excess in the beginning, according to the sinning of sin.

Therefore, regarding the penalty of becoming a sin in excess in the time to come, he signifies this by saying: 'that sin may become a sin in excess through the commandment.' If they were to say: 'And how could it be good and just? And how is the commandment and the law holy, when through their occasion sin became a sin in excess?' Let them listen to this: that if something is being harmed, the occasion through which it is harmed is already bad and evil. Just as we do not say the sun is evil just because those who gaze at it without end and without measure are harmed in their eyes. Nor do we say the Son of God is bad and evil just because the devil has become a sin in excess by opposing the Son of God.

I know that the good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh (Rom 7:21). This is explained through the person of Adam. And that, having been deprived of God to have within himself, he exchanged true life for death—for death did not hold only the common members of it, but also the disobedience invading his soul. For above all, death ruled before the arrival of Christ, having disobedience as the law and scepter of its own kingdom. But the kingdom of death is not without a ruler or unbegotten; for to die happens from the living, and to disobey happens from the obedience of subjects.

For the willing is possible for me, but the doing of the good is not. For what I want as good, this I do not do, but what I hate, this I practice (Rom 7:15). If the willing alone is in us, but the doing of the thing willed as good is not in us, then the good God sent his consubstantial souls into bodies in vain; for they do not practice what they love and what is with them, but only they will; perhaps even that [willing] is not, for it is unclear. If this is true, I will say according to the impious: then the good was not and will not be in life, nor did anyone ever act it, if they take as a refutation of the good and the beautiful against every man, that what I want as good, this I do not do, but what I hate, this [I do].
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Dwelling of Sin
english: I do [it]. But where, even in the life of men, have the names of virtues been found? If they are indeed active in doing what is good, even if those doing this were few, will not all say so? Yet we know that good does not dwell in us; for whatever they desired to be good, this is what they practice. But if those who are active in the good exist in the flesh doing this, and those who do not do this but are in the flesh doing evil, is it not the flesh that is the cause of the good not happening by turning away, but rather the softness of their soul?

For if to those desiring to do the good, evil is a neighbor, and likewise to those desiring to do evil, good is not a guest, yet having foreseen and having intended, they arrive at such great activities, is it not that our bodies are not evil in nature and essence? For of our practical actions, counsel and will go before, the soul having this faculty of mind, being able to flow toward the actions it wills. Now I no longer work this, but the sin dwelling in me. He explained through this logical point that the flesh is not naturally evil; for it is not the flesh in which we are surrounded that dwells in us, but the devil dwelling in lawlessness. For that which I say is: Christ dwells in every righteous person working the good, while I think the same manner of way the devil dwells in every evildoer.

Therefore, it is not that we are evil because we have flesh, but the sin dwelling in us, being something else besides the flesh and the soul of the man; for it is said especially in the soul that the devil dwells in, according to how Satan entered into the heart of Judas (John 13:2), and according to Ananias, 'Why has Satan filled your heart?' (Acts 5:3). And it is indeed good to say, 'I no longer work this, but the sin dwelling in me'; for the preparation goes before the work much like, so to speak, the preparation of a house or a temple; and the preparation is that which is the groundwork of the matter. Thus, the sin dwelling in those who sin—that is, the devil—concedes in our thoughts that he prepares beforehand the idea of the evil to come, the construction, of the soul cooperating with him in the wickedness, just as the womb of a female prepares for the sowing to be brought to completion.

And since evil thoughts come out of the heart (Matthew 12:34), from the seizure occurring of the devil, the divine word has cried out: taking thoughts captive and lifting up every height against the knowledge of God (2 Corinthians 10:5). Just as for the well-disposed souls the Holy Spirit is said to toil together, according to the saying, 'I have labored more than all,' not I, but the grace of God with me, so also, if a yielding soul is persuaded by the incitements of the devil, it has a co-worker in the evil, the devil himself; for he also prepared beforehand in it the pattern of the coming sin. For this reason it is said, 'I no longer work this, but the sin dwelling in me.'
